A bicycle gear system allows riders to adjust the effort needed to pedal based on terrain, speed, and personal preference. It consists of a front chainring (attached to the pedals) and multiple rear sprockets (on the rear wheel), connected by a chain. The gear ratio—calculated by dividing the number of teeth on the front chainring by the number of teeth on the rear sprocket—determines how much force is transferred to the rear wheel.

When the rider pedals, the chain transfers power from the front chainring to the rear sprocket, turning the rear wheel. Larger front chainrings or smaller rear sprockets increase the gear ratio, making it harder to pedal but allowing faster speeds—ideal for flat terrain or downhill.
